rationale: This qualitative single-site case study examines an NGO-led (CURE) water and sanitation proof-of-concept project in an informal housing cluster in NOIDA, Uttar Pradesh, drawing on CURE project reports and personal observation. Multiple governance mechanisms are co-central: the central thesis evaluates private market-based contracting and community-funded service provision versus public municipal delivery (regulatory_model_ownership), facilitated by NGO-led participatory mobilisation and repeated bureaucratic navigation with local authorities (participation_assistance), necessitated by municipal refusal to provide infrastructure due to illegal settlement status (eligibility_status_documentation) and enabled by non-obstructive street-level official flexibility on solid waste and independently funded works (discretion_accommodation). The primary outcome evaluated is functional sanitation, drainage cleanliness, waste collection reliability, and water quality conditions in the settlement (effective_access).
